cases.presenting_complaint: Constant excessive worry about multiple things including family health, finances, and work for over a year
cases.associated: Restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, sleep disturbance (difficulty falling asleep due to worry). Worry is difficult to control and shifts between topics
cases.risk_factors: Perfectionism, family history of anxiety in mother, recent increased work responsibilities, caring for aging parent
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-groomed but appears tense. Behavior: Restless, fidgety. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Constantly on edge, always waiting for something bad to happen'. Affect: Anxious, worried. Thought: Excessive worry about minor matters, catastrophizing, 'what if' thinking. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reduced concentration. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: GAD-7: 17/21 (severe anxiety). PHQ-9: 8/27 (mild depression - common comorbidity). TSH, ECG: normal. Caffeine intake: high (6 cups coffee/day)
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Anxiety may be protective factor
cases.explanation: GAD characterized by excessive anxiety and worry about multiple events/activities for ≥6 months, difficult to control, with ≥3 of 6 associated symptoms (restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance). This patient has all 6. GAD is chronic, often begins in 20s-30s, and causes significant distress and impairment. High comorbidity with depression (50-60%). Distinguished from normal worry by excessiveness, uncontrollability, and impairment
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about GAD and anxiety; (2) FIRST-LINE: CBT for GAD - challenge catastrophic thinking, worry exposure, problem-solving; (3) SSRI or SNRI (sertraline 50-200mg, escitalopram 10-20mg, venlafaxine XR 75-225mg, duloxetine 60-120mg); (4) Reduce caffeine intake (currently excessive); (5) Relaxation techniques - progressive muscle relaxation, breathing exercises; (6) Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy; (7) Regular exercise; (8) Sleep hygiene; (9) Avoid benzodiazepines for chronic use (dependence risk); (10) Address life stressors (parent care - respite services); (11) Regular follow-up; (12) Long-term treatment often needed (years)

cases.presenting_complaint: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks and fear of having attacks in public, leading to avoidance of shopping centers, public transport, and crowds
cases.duration: 2 years since first panic attack, progressive avoidance over past year
cases.associated: Panic attacks: sudden onset of intense fear with palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, derealization, fear of dying. Attacks last 10-20 minutes. Now avoids situations where escape difficult or help unavailable. Becoming housebound
cases.risk_factors: First panic attack occurred on crowded train, subsequent attacks in similar situations, family history of panic disorder in aunt, recent relationship stress
cases.mse: Appearance: Anxious. Behavior: Hypervigilant, checking exits. Speech: Normal but anxious. Mood: 'Terrified of having another attack, feels safer at home'. Affect: Anxious. Thought: Fear of panic attacks, catastrophic interpretation of bodily sensations. Perception: Depersonalization during attacks. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - knows fear excessive but feels real
cases.investigations: Panic Disorder Severity Scale: 18/28 (moderate-severe). Agoraphobia scale: severe avoidance. ECG: normal sinus rhythm (to reassure about cardiac symptoms). Thyroid function: normal
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Panic disorder associated with increased suicide risk, especially with comorbid depression. Monitor for demoralization
cases.explanation: Panic Disorder: recurrent unexpected panic attacks (discrete periods of intense fear with physical and cognitive symptoms) plus ≥1 month of persistent concern about attacks or maladaptive behavioral change. Agoraphobia: fear/anxiety about ≥2 of 5 situations (public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds, outside home alone) due to fear of panic symptoms and inability to escape. This patient has both. Avoidance provides short-term relief but maintains disorder long-term through negative reinforcement
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about panic attacks (not dangerous, time-limited, body's alarm system); (2) CBT for panic disorder and agoraphobia (GOLD STANDARD): interoceptive exposure (induce panic sensations), cognitive restructuring (challenge catastrophic misinterpretations), in vivo exposure (graduated facing of feared situations); (3) SSRI (sertraline 50-200mg or paroxetine 20-60mg - specifically indicated for panic); (4) Short-term benzodiazepine for acute attacks only (alprazolam 0.5mg PRN) but avoid long-term; (5) Breathing retraining (though avoid over-focus on breathing); (6) Graded exposure hierarchy starting with easier situations; (7) Consider involving family member for support during exposures; (8) Address relationship stress; (9) Regular exercise; (10) Avoid caffeine, alcohol; (11) 12-16 sessions CBT typically needed; (12) Medication for 12-24 months then gradual taper; (13) Relapse prevention planning

cases.presenting_complaint: Sudden episodes of intense fear with heart racing, sweating, and feeling like I'm dying, occurring unpredictably for 6 months
cases.associated: Panic attacks occur unexpectedly, even waking from sleep. Symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, fear of dying/losing control. Attacks peak at 10 minutes. Constant worry about next attack but no avoidance of situations
cases.risk_factors: High-stress job (investment banking), poor sleep, excessive caffeine use, recent death of colleague from heart attack (triggered health anxiety)
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-groomed, appears anxious. Behavior: Normal. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Constantly worried I'm going to have another attack'. Affect: Anxious. Thought: Health anxiety, fear of heart attack despite normal tests, hypervigilance to bodily sensations. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial
cases.investigations: Multiple ED visits for chest pain - all cardiac workup normal (ECG, troponin, echo). 24-hour Holter: occasional benign PVCs only. GAD-7: 14/21. Panic Disorder Severity Scale: 12/28 (moderate). Agoraphobic avoidance: none
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation but significant impact on quality of life
cases.explanation: Panic Disorder without agoraphobia: recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus persistent concern/worry about attacks or their consequences (fear of heart attack, 'going crazy') or maladaptive behavioral change, BUT without agoraphobic avoidance. Panic attacks are false alarms - sympathetic nervous system activation without real danger. Common misattribution is cardiac disease leading to repeated ED visits. Colleague's death from heart attack created health anxiety vulnerability
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about panic attacks - not dangerous, false alarm, cannot cause heart attack/death; (2) Review normal cardiac investigations to provide reassurance; (3) CBT for panic disorder: cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretations ('racing heart means heart attack' → 'racing heart is anxiety response'), interoceptive exposure (deliberately induce panic sensations like hyperventilation, running in place to learn they're not dangerous); (4) SSRI: sertraline 50-200mg or paroxetine 20-60mg; (5) Reduce/eliminate caffeine (major trigger); (6) Sleep optimization; (7) Stress management and work-life balance; (8) Regular exercise (reduces panic frequency); (9) Benzodiazepines PRN only if needed initially (alprazolam 0.5mg), aim to discontinue; (10) Avoid alcohol; (11) 12-16 week CBT course; (12) Consider occupational health referral for work stress; (13) Monitor for development of agoraphobia; (14) Maintenance treatment 12-24 months

cases.presenting_complaint: Intense fear of social situations and being judged by others, leading to avoidance of work meetings, social events, and eating in public
cases.associated: Fear of embarrassment, humiliation, or negative evaluation in social situations. Physical symptoms in social situations: blushing, sweating, trembling, nausea. Avoids presentations, meetings, dating, restaurants. Severe impact on career and relationships
cases.risk_factors: Childhood bullying, shy temperament from early childhood, family history of anxiety, socially isolated, unemployment due to anxiety
cases.mse: Appearance: Avoids eye contact, appears uncomfortable. Behavior: Anxious, self-conscious during interview. Speech: Quiet, hesitant. Mood: 'Terrified of what people think of me'. Affect: Anxious, restricted. Thought: Excessive self-focus, assumption others judge negatively, mind-reading. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - recognizes fear is excessive
cases.investigations: Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale: 92/144 (severe). PHQ-9: 14/27 (comorbid depression common). Alcohol use: increased use for 'Dutch courage' before social situations (warning sign)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Comorbid depression, social isolation, unemployment. Chronic impairment leads to hopelessness
cases.explanation: Social Anxiety Disorder: marked fear/anxiety about social situations where individual may be scrutinized, fears negative evaluation, social situations almost always provoke anxiety, situations avoided or endured with intense anxiety, fear disproportionate to threat, ≥6 months duration, significant impairment. Most common anxiety disorder. Onset typically adolescence. Untreated leads to depression, substance use, occupational impairment. Safety behaviors (avoiding eye contact, rehearsing speech) maintain anxiety by preventing disconfirmation of fears
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about social anxiety; (2) CBT for social anxiety (GOLD STANDARD): identify negative automatic thoughts ('everyone thinks I'm stupid'), cognitive restructuring, attention training (shift from self-focus to external), drop safety behaviors, graded exposure hierarchy (start with easier situations like asking stranger for time, progress to presentations); (3) SSRI: paroxetine, sertraline, or escitalopram 10-20mg (all effective for social anxiety); OR venlafaxine XR 75-225mg; (4) Beta-blocker (propranolol 10-40mg) for performance anxiety PRN but NOT primary treatment; (5) Avoid alcohol (self-medication worsens long-term); (6) Social skills training if deficits present; (7) Assertiveness training; (8) Vocational rehabilitation; (9) Address comorbid depression; (10) Group CBT particularly effective (exposure to being observed); (11) 16-20 sessions typically needed; (12) Long-term treatment often required; (13) Relapse prevention

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe anxiety specifically about performing or speaking in front of others, affecting work presentations
cases.duration: Since university (12 years), impacting career advancement
cases.associated: Fear limited to performance situations (presentations, public speaking, performing music). Intense anxiety in anticipation and during performance: trembling, voice shaking, blushing, mind going blank. Otherwise comfortable in social interactions. Avoids situations requiring presentations, limiting career
cases.risk_factors: Humiliating experience during school presentation (laughed at), perfectionism, works in field requiring presentations (marketing), otherwise socially confident
cases.mse: Appearance: Professional, good eye contact in one-on-one setting. Behavior: Comfortable in interview. Speech: Normal in conversation. Mood: 'Fine usually, but panic at thought of presentations'. Affect: Euthymic except when discussing performances. Thought: Fear of visible anxiety symptoms, worry about negative evaluation of performance. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Excellent
cases.investigations: Brief Social Phobia Scale: Elevated only for performance situations. General social functioning: normal. No comorbid depression. Propranolol use: self-prescribed, uses before every presentation
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. Good functioning except specific situations
cases.explanation: Performance-only social anxiety disorder: fear limited to speaking/performing in public. DSM-5 specifier: 'performance only' if fear restricted to performing or speaking. Less pervasive than generalized social anxiety. Often begins after humiliating performance experience. Physical symptoms (trembling, blushing, voice shaking) are feared as they may be noticed by audience. Perfectionism often comorbid. Avoidance limits career advancement despite talent
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation - performance anxiety is common and treatable; (2) CBT focused on performance situations: video feedback (record presentation, watch to challenge catastrophic predictions - usually not as bad as feared), cognitive restructuring ('visible anxiety means failure' → 'most people don't notice or care'), exposure hierarchy of performance situations; (3) Acceptance-based approach - accept anxiety rather than fight it; (4) Beta-blocker (propranolol 20-40mg) 30-60 minutes before performance - reduces physical symptoms, can use long-term for performances; (5) SSRI less essential for performance-only type unless symptoms severe or spreading; (6) Public speaking courses or Toastmasters; (7) Practice exposures using video; (8) Address perfectionism; (9) Shift focus from internal (how I feel/look) to external (content, audience); (10) Drop safety behaviors (over-preparation, avoiding eye contact); (11) Usually shorter treatment than generalized social anxiety; (12) Good prognosis with treatment

cases.presenting_complaint: Extreme fear of dogs since being bitten as a child, now affecting daily life as cannot visit friends with dogs or walk in parks
cases.associated: Immediate intense fear upon seeing dogs, even small/friendly ones. Avoidance of parks, streets where dogs common, friends' homes. Physical symptoms: palpitations, sweating, urge to flee. Recognizes fear is excessive but cannot control it
cases.risk_factors: Dog bite requiring stitches age 7, no previous exposure to dogs before incident, mother also fears dogs (modeling)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Normal. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Fine except around dogs'. Affect: Anxious when discussing dogs. Thought: Overestimation of danger from dogs, belief all dogs may attack. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - knows fear is excessive
cases.investigations: Specific Phobia Questionnaire (Dog): 28/35 (severe). Otherwise no psychiatric symptoms. Functioning normal except phobia-related avoidance
cases.explanation: Specific Phobia (Animal Type): marked fear/anxiety about specific object (dogs), object almost always provokes immediate fear, actively avoided or endured with intense anxiety, fear disproportionate to actual danger, ≥6 months, causes impairment or distress. Animal phobias typically begin in childhood, often after negative experience. Can persist lifelong if untreated. Relatively circumscribed impact unless phobic object commonly encountered. Classical conditioning (dog bite) plus vicarious learning (mother's fear) contributed to development
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about specific phobias and maintenance through avoidance; (2) Exposure therapy (TREATMENT OF CHOICE): systematic desensitization - gradual exposure starting with images/videos of dogs, then small dogs at distance, progress to small dogs nearby, larger dogs at distance, larger dogs nearby, eventually touching/petting dogs. Each step repeated until anxiety decreases before progressing; (3) Cognitive restructuring: challenge probability estimates ('most dogs are friendly', 'only 0.001% of dog encounters result in bites'); (4) Relaxation training to use during exposures; (5) Virtual reality exposure if available; (6) Dog safety education (how to approach dogs safely, read dog body language); (7) Medication generally NOT needed for specific phobias (exposure therapy highly effective); (8) Benzodiazepine PRN could be used during exposures but may prevent full habituation; (9) 4-8 sessions typically sufficient; (10) Excellent prognosis - specific phobias respond very well to exposure therapy; (11) Relapse uncommon if fully treated

cases.presenting_complaint: Intense fear of flying preventing business travel and family vacations
cases.associated: Avoids flying - takes trains for work travel (8-10 hour trips), family doesn't take vacations requiring flights. When forced to fly: severe anticipatory anxiety weeks before, panic during flight (especially takeoff, landing, turbulence), physical symptoms (palpitations, sweating, hyperventilation). Career impacted
cases.risk_factors: Severe turbulence on flight 10 years ago (plane dropped suddenly, people screamed, oxygen masks deployed), subsequent fear generalized to all flights, avoidance maintained phobia
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate, professional. Behavior: Normal. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Embarrassed about fear, but can't control it'. Affect: Anxious discussing flying. Thought: Overestimates risk of crashes, catastrophizes about turbulence. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: Flight Anxiety Questionnaire: Severe anxiety all phases. Otherwise psychiatrically well. No other phobias. Previous failed attempts with alcohol pre-flight and diazepam (remained highly anxious)
cases.explanation: Specific Phobia - Situational Type (flying): situational phobias include flying, enclosed spaces, heights, driving, bridges. Often begin in adulthood following traumatic experience (unlike animal phobias which begin in childhood). Fear maintained by avoidance and catastrophic thinking. Distinguishable from panic disorder as fear is cued (flying) not spontaneous. Flying phobia affects 2-5% population. Interferes with work, family, opportunities
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about flight safety statistics, how planes work, what turbulence is (uncomfortable but not dangerous); (2) Exposure therapy (in vivo): gradual hierarchy - visiting airport without flying, sitting in stationary plane, short flight, longer flight, flight in turbulence season. Each step repeated until anxiety decreases; (3) Virtual reality exposure therapy for flying (effective and accessible); (4) Cognitive restructuring: challenge catastrophic thoughts ('turbulence will crash plane' → 'turbulence is normal, planes designed for it'), probability overestimation; (5) Anxiety management techniques: breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation; (6) Many airlines offer fear of flying courses combining education and exposure; (7) Aviation education from pilot perspective helpful; (8) Short-term benzodiazepine for flights (alprazolam 0.5-1mg) can be bridge while doing therapy, but avoid long-term as prevents habituation; (9) Avoid alcohol (worsens anxiety long-term); (10) 6-10 sessions typically sufficient; (11) Booster sessions if needed; (12) Good prognosis with exposure therapy

cases.presenting_complaint: Fear of being in situations where escape might be difficult, leading to avoidance of public transport, shopping centers, and leaving home alone for 3 years
cases.associated: Fear of being outside home alone, using public transport, being in crowds, open spaces. Fears becoming dizzy/having medical emergency with no help available. Requires husband accompany her everywhere. Becoming increasingly housebound. No panic attacks
cases.risk_factors: Began after fainting episode in supermarket (due to dehydration), fear developed that would faint again, gradual avoidance spread to other situations, husband retired (enabling avoidance by accompanying her)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Anxious. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Trapped, afraid to leave house alone'. Affect: Anxious, somewhat depressed. Thought: Fear of fainting or medical emergency in public, belief cannot cope alone. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - knows fear excessive but feels real
cases.investigations: Agoraphobia Scale: Severe avoidance in all domains. No panic attacks on detailed history. Comorbid depression developing from restricted lifestyle. Medical evaluation for fainting: vasovagal syncope due to dehydration - benign cause identified
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Demoralization from restricted life. Feeling burdensome to husband
cases.explanation: Agoraphobia can occur without panic disorder. DSM-5 recognizes agoraphobia as separate diagnosis. Fear/anxiety about ≥2 of 5 situations (public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, crowds, outside home alone) due to fear of difficult-to-escape situations and fear of incapacitating symptoms (dizziness, falling, incontinence) or embarrassment. Avoidance or requires companion. This patient's agoraphobia began after fainting episode - conditioning of fear. Different mechanism than panic disorder-related agoraphobia. Husband's retirement enabled avoidance
cases.management: (1) Medical reassurance about fainting episode (benign vasovagal, easily prevented with hydration); (2) Psychoeducation about agoraphobia and maintenance through avoidance; (3) Graded in vivo exposure (ESSENTIAL): create hierarchy from easiest (walk to end of driveway alone) to hardest (public transport alone). Each step repeated until anxiety decreases. Initially may need husband present but gradually fade his presence; (4) CBT: cognitive restructuring of probability of fainting and catastrophic consequences; (5) Interoceptive exposure to dizziness (head rolling, spinning) to reduce fear of sensation; (6) Drop safety behaviors (hypervigilance, carrying water bottle everywhere, scanning for exits); (7) SSRI if comorbid depression significant (sertraline 50-150mg); (8) Address enabling - husband needs to support exposure not avoidance; (9) Hydration strategies to prevent actual fainting; (10) Regular exercise to improve confidence in body; (11) 16-20 sessions CBT typically needed; (12) Occupational therapy for activity scheduling; (13) Social re-engagement; (14) Good prognosis with treatment though often chronic if untreated

cases.presenting_complaint: Excessive anxiety about being separated from parents, particularly mother, affecting ability to move out or maintain romantic relationships
cases.duration: Lifelong but seeking help now due to relationship problems
cases.associated: Extreme distress when separated from mother, excessive worry about harm coming to parents, reluctance to sleep away from home, avoids travel or overnight work trips, calls mother multiple times daily, relationships ended as partners felt 'third wheel', nightmares about separation
cases.risk_factors: Anxious attachment since childhood, overprotective parenting, mother has chronic illness (creates worry about her health), no siblings, previous attempts to move out resulted in panic and return home within days
cases.mse: Appearance: Younger than age, appropriate. Behavior: Cooperative but anxious. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I know I should be independent but I can't stand being away from my parents'. Affect: Anxious. Thought: Excessive worry about parents' safety, catastrophizing. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - recognizes impact on life but fears separation
cases.investigations: Adult Separation Anxiety Questionnaire: Severe symptoms. GAD-7: 13/21 (generalized anxiety may be comorbid). Attachment style: anxious-preoccupied. Developmental history: no major separations in childhood, mother always present
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation but relationship distress
cases.explanation: Separation Anxiety Disorder: excessive fear/anxiety about separation from attachment figures, inappropriate for developmental level, ≥6 months in adults (4 weeks in children). Symptoms: worry about harm to attachment figure, reluctance to be away, fear of being alone, nightmares about separation, physical symptoms when separated. Typically begins childhood (7% of children) but can persist into adulthood or rarely begin in adulthood. Adult prevalence ~2-4%. Interferes with independence, work, romantic relationships. Differential includes dependent personality disorder (broader pattern beyond separation anxiety)
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about separation anxiety in adults; (2) CBT: cognitive restructuring of overestimated danger to parents and inability to cope alone, graduated exposure to separation (start with hours alone, progress to overnight, then travel), develop independent coping skills; (3) Family therapy: address enmeshment, establish healthy boundaries, parent education (need to support independence not dependence); (4) Attachment-based therapy to address anxious attachment patterns; (5) SSRI may help anxiety symptoms (sertraline or escitalopram); (6) Skills training: problem-solving, emotion regulation; (7) Encourage independent activities and friendships; (8) Graded independence plan: move to nearby apartment before distant city; (9) Address parents' role in maintaining anxiety (reassurance-seeking, frequent contact); (10) Mindfulness for anxiety tolerance; (11) Support for romantic relationship if currently in one; (12) Long-term therapy often needed (rooted in attachment patterns); (13) Monitor for comorbid depression; (14) Good prognosis with treatment but requires active work on independence

cases.presenting_complaint: Unable to speak in academic settings (lectures, seminars) despite normal speech at home and with close friends since childhood
cases.duration: Since primary school (13+ years), persisting into university
cases.associated: Complete inability to speak in classroom settings, during presentations, to authority figures (professors). Can write, use gestures. Speaks normally at home, with family, close friends. Extreme anxiety in situations where expected to speak. Academic performance affected (cannot participate, ask questions, give presentations)
cases.risk_factors: Extremely shy temperament from infancy, social anxiety since childhood, cultural background (immigrant family, English second language), previous bullying about accent
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate, avoids eye contact. Behavior: Communicates through writing during assessment, very anxious. Speech: Unable to speak initially, whispers with great effort after 30 minutes, reports normal speech at home. Mood: (written) 'Frustrated, embarrassed, want to speak but can't'. Affect: Anxious, distressed. Thought: Fear of negative evaluation, fear of speaking itself. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: Clinical observation: selective mutism confirmed. Underlying social anxiety disorder diagnosed. No speech or hearing problems. IQ testing: above average (non-verbal). Video from home: speaks normally with family
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Significant impairment, hopelessness about future, social isolation beyond family
cases.explanation: Selective Mutism: consistent failure to speak in specific social situations (where speaking expected - school, work) despite speaking in other situations, ≥1 month duration, interferes with achievement. Not due to communication disorder or psychosis. Typically begins age 2-5 but can persist into adulthood if untreated (~1% of children, rare in adults). Conceptualized as extreme form of social anxiety - speaking in feared situations provokes overwhelming anxiety. Speaking failure reinforced by immediate anxiety relief (negative reinforcement) but maintains long-term problem. In adults, extremely impairing for education, employment, relationships
cases.management: (1) Conceptualize as extreme social anxiety with learned behavioral component; (2) Multimodal treatment: CBT for social anxiety + behavioral interventions for speaking; (3) Graduated exposure hierarchy: whisper to therapist → speak quietly to therapist → speak in small group → speak in classroom → presentations. Use stimulus fading (start with situation can speak, gradually change to harder situation); (4) Contingency management: positive reinforcement for speaking attempts; (5) SSRI (high-dose often needed - sertraline 150-200mg, paroxetine 40-60mg); (6) Involve university: accommodations initially (written work, small groups) while working toward speaking, but goal is to fade accommodations; (7) Self-modeling videos (record speaking at home, watch daily); (8) Address underlying social anxiety; (9) Speech and language therapist involvement; (10) Group therapy for social anxiety (exposure to being observed); (11) Address cultural factors and bullying history; (12) Family involvement; (13) Long-term intensive treatment needed; (14) Prognosis more guarded in adults than children (chronic pattern) but improvement possible with intensive treatment
